title: Beyond Data Centers: Growing Out of the Middle-Tech Trap
gist: Jonathan Dason argues that Malaysia's data-center boom risks deepening a 'middle-technology trap' of hosting foreign technology without owning IP. He says Malaysia should hedge between the US and China and build 'Made by Malaysia' capability from its semiconductor ATP base into IC design and edge AI, with ambitious 2030 targets but significant execution risk.

insights.claim: The middle-technology trap occurs when countries adopt foreign technology but fail to develop domestic innovation and intellectual property, leaving them confined to lower-value segments of global value chains.
insights.so_what: A lens for judging whether FDI-led tech booms in emerging markets translate into durable domestic value capture.
insights.quote: The middle-technology trap occurs when countries adopt foreign technology but fail to develop domestic innovation and intellectual property.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: A Malaysian technology CEO said the country optimized for process excellence while outsourcing intellectual property and product design to multinational corporations.
insights.so_what: Malaysian tech value accrues mostly to foreign MNCs rather than local IP owners.
insights.quote: “(the country) optimized for the ‘how’ (process excellence) while outsourcing the ‘what’ (intellectual property and product design) to multinational corporations.”
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: Malaysia can host the AI boom by importing chips, building data centers, and deploying foreign foundation models, reaping short-term productivity gains without ever owning any of the underlying technology.
insights.so_what: Data-center-led growth in Malaysia may have limited long-term value capture for the domestic economy.
insights.quote: reaping short-term productivity gains yet never owning a piece of the underlying technology
insights.locator: The advent of AI adds a new dimension
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: Malaysia's 1990s Multimedia Super Corridor attracted investment but delivered mixed results and fell short of its innovation ambitions.
insights.so_what: Past industrial-policy underdelivery is a base rate for skepticism about Malaysia's new AI plans.
insights.locator: Turning “Made in Malaysia” into “Made by Malaysia”
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

themes.theme: Hedging between US and China stacks

insights.claim: Malaysia sits amid a US-China technology competition in which each power is building its own AI stack, and it is neither economically efficient nor technologically feasible for Malaysia to compete with both across the AI value chain.
insights.so_what: Middle powers will specialize in niches rather than build full AI stacks, sustaining the dominance of US and Chinese platform providers.
insights.quote: it is not economically efficient, nor is it technologically feasible, for the country to compete with both the United States and China across the AI value chain
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: Even though DeepSeek's V3 frontier model reportedly cost under USD 6 million to develop, that sum is not easily footed by a developing country like Malaysia.
insights.so_what: Lower frontier-model costs still do not make sovereign frontier AI viable for most emerging economies.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: Malaysia's sensible strategy is to stay neutral, building domestic capabilities in strategic segments while selectively integrating foreign capital and technology from both the US and China.
insights.so_what: Malaysia will likely keep courting both US and Chinese tech investment, exposing it to export-control and secondary-pressure risks.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: 'Made by Malaysia' carries a second meaning of technological sovereignty, requiring domestic control only over critical parts of the stack such as sensitive data, essential infrastructure, and applications used in national decision-making, rather than autarky.
insights.so_what: Foreign AI vendors may face localization requirements in Malaysian critical systems while the broader market stays open.
insights.locator: This is where the dual meaning
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: Malaysia is the 6th largest semiconductor exporter globally and accounts for 13% of global assembly, testing, and packaging (ATP) volume.
insights.so_what: Malaysia is a key node in back-end semiconductor supply chains, relevant to advanced packaging demand from AI chips.
insights.quote: Malaysia is the 6th largest semiconductor exporter globally, accounting for 13% of global assembly, testing, and packaging (ATP) volume
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: Malaysia aims to use its semiconductor ATP base to move into adjacent higher-value segments such as integrated circuit design, with firms like SykeChip, Oppstar, and Vitrox expanding its technical niche.
insights.so_what: Malaysian IC-design and equipment names are the listed vehicles for a move up the semiconductor value chain.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: SykeChip, which listed on Bursa Malaysia in 2026, developed the MARS1000 edge AI processor that processes data on-device to reduce latency and protect privacy without internet dependency.
insights.so_what: Edge AI chips are an emerging local IP play in Malaysia's equity market.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

themes.theme: Malaysia's 2030 AI targets and execution risk

insights.claim: Malaysia's 2030 targets include raising the AI-anchored digital economy to 30% of GDP, reaching the top 25 of the IMD World Digital Competitiveness Ranking, ranking in the top 10 of Stanford's AI Index, reskilling 700,000 workers, creating 500,000 jobs, financing 5,000 local tech companies, and producing five digital unicorns.
insights.so_what: Quantified targets give investors benchmarks to track Malaysia's AI policy delivery and potential state financing flows.
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: Malaysia's national AI plans do not aim to build the next Nvidia, Anthropic, or Moonshot AI, but to complement existing strengths along the AI value chain without competing directly with the great powers.
insights.so_what: Malaysia is positioned as a complement to, not a competitor of, frontier AI leaders.
insights.quote: it is clear that Malaysia does not seek to build the next Nvidia, Anthropic, or Moonshot AI
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute

insights.claim: Malaysia's AI industrial policy faces execution risk because AI may advance faster than the government can reskill workers and regulate, and the state cannot reliably predict technological trajectories.
insights.so_what: Discount official AI targets; delivery shortfalls are plausible given past precedent.
insights.quote: AI may advance faster than the speed at which the government can reskill workers and regulate new developments
insights.speaker: Asia Society Policy Institute
